source.title: Universal Neurons in GPT2 Language Models
source.authors: Wes Gurnee; T. Horsley; Zifan Carl Guo; Tara Rezaei Kheirkhah; Qinyi Sun; W. Hathaway; Neel Nanda; Dimitris Bertsimas

page_placements.theme: Universality and reproducibility of units across seeds, architectures, dictionary fits and paraphrased inputs

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies cross-seed activation universality and interprets selected neurons, but does not measure the share of neuron poles with one or two jobs, test explanations on held-out activations, or evaluate the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's conclusion that neurons are not the appropriate unit for most network behaviours is relevant discussion, but its universality measure is not a test of the listed versions' job-share or explanation-quality measures. Its numerical universality results are recorded as findings about the claim's subject, not as evidence for or against those versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures cross-seed activation universality: neurons whose activations correlate with a neuron in models trained from other seeds, above a rotated-basis baseline. It then interprets only the selected universal neurons. It never estimates what share of all neurons, or neuron poles, have one main job, two jobs or none. It does not score explanations on held-out activations, study InceptionV1 or pose, compare architectures or tools, or build attribution graphs. Its claim that neurons are 'not the appropriate unit' rests on low universality, not on an interpretability audit. So it bears on no listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find only about 1–5% of neurons are universal across seeds. They call this 'another piece of evidence' that neurons are not the right unit for most behaviour. They add that the few universal neurons are often interpretable, fall into families, and some have clear functional roles (entropy, attention deactivation, prediction/suppression).
record.recipe_differences: Uses cross-seed maximum activation correlations over a large token corpus, with a random-rotation baseline, then manually examines selected neurons. It does not use the Qwen3-32B pole audit or held-out explanation-scoring procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported universal-neuron share varies by model: GPT2-small is reported at 4.16%, versus 1.23% for GPT2-medium and 1.26% for Pythia-160M, using the stated excess-correlation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Only about 1–5% of neurons pass the excess-correlation universality threshold (4.16% GPT2-small-a, about 1.23% GPT2-medium-a, 1.26% Pythia-160M).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Few individual neurons have activation patterns replicated across random seeds of the same architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Universal neurons have high pre-activation skew and kurtosis and large negative bias. Non-universal neurons have skew near 0 and kurtosis near 3, Gaussian-like (Section 4.2, Fig. 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation statistics suggestive of monosemanticity concentrate in universal neurons; most neurons look statistically Gaussian.

fits_no_version.finding: Universal neurons selected by ϱ>0.5 usually have clear interpretations (unigram, alphabet, previous-token, position, syntax, semantic, prediction/suppression families).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons that are universal across seeds tend to be interpretable.

record.problems: The study focuses on relatively small models and random-seed variation within model families. Its interpretation analysis is manual and focused on selected universal neurons, and the authors note that this narrow focus may obscure much of the network's computation. Its results do not estimate the fraction of all neurons with a single main job.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were extracted: the paper's downstream functional-role examples and neuron statistics do not measure the listed versions' job shares or explanation accuracy.

untested.parts: No share of Qwen3-32B neuron poles with one job, two jobs or none; no audit of all neurons.
No interpretability shares in any model. GPT2-small, GPT2-medium and Pythia-160M are measured for universality only; no MoE or large-scale models.
No InceptionV1, cat-and-car neurons, pose or recursive generalization.
No comparison of interpretable shares across architectures, regularization or tool quality.
No neuron-based attribution graphs and no replacement-model comparison.
Explanations are not tested against where neurons fire on new data. The variance-reduction tests are applied only to universal neurons and no aggregate is reported.

record.verdict_notes: The study's relevance to the claim is indirect. Universality is not the same as interpretability, and the authors do not measure interpretability among non-universal neurons. Their speculation that larger models have fewer universal neurons cites Bills et al. (an original source) and is not tested here. Keep it as discussion only.

versions.untested_parts: Does not estimate the share of all neuron poles with one or two main jobs or the share not understood; does not audit Qwen3-32B or test explanations on held-out activations.
Measures cross-seed activation universality, not whether similar shares of neurons have one main job across models; does not study MoE models or trillion-parameter models.
Does not study InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not compare interpretability shares across architectures, regularization choices, or tool quality, or estimate the stated InceptionV1-sized vision-model shares.
Does not evaluate attribution graphs or compare neuron-based explanations with a trained replacement model and reconstruction error.
Does not test explanations against where neurons fire on new examples.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: GPT2-medium-a
rows.operation_detail: Measured maximum cross-model neuron activation correlations over 100 million tokens and computed excess correlation relative to a random rotated-basis baseline.

conditions.value: 100 million tokens from the Pile test set

rows.measure: Count of neurons above the excess-correlation threshold
rows.baseline: Random rotated-basis maximum correlations; numeric baseline share not stated
rows.value: 1253 out of 98304 neurons (1.23%, as reported in the paper's comparison)
rows.note: The paper calls these neurons universal under its cross-seed activation-correlation definition. This is not a measurement of how many neurons have one main job.
rows.check: The count is right (1253 of 98304, ϱ>0.5, GPT2-medium-a), but 1253/98304 is about 1.27%, not 1.23%. The paper's 1.23% is its own stated GPT2-medium figure; the small mismatch is in the paper. The measure is cross-seed universality, not job share.

source_check.correct: 1253 of 98304 neurons in GPT2-medium-a have excess correlation >0.5 (the paper separately reports 1.23%; 1253/98304 is about 1.27%)
source_check.problem: Minor: the paper's 1.23% does not match 1253/98304 (1.27%); the record copies both.

relation.reason: The study discusses whether neurons are interpretable units (polysemanticity, universal neurons as monosemantic candidates) without testing the claim. It predates the claim's essay.

tranche.reason: The study measures cross-seed activation universality, not the share of neurons (or poles) with one main job. Its interpretability judgements are qualitative and cover only universal neurons, so it tests no version.

source_check.notes: R3 duplicates R1: 1.23% is the GPT2-medium-a share against models b-e, and the paper's own 1.23% doesn't match 1253/98304 (1.27%). The authors hypothesised that universality approximates the number of meaningful neurons, and they read 1-5% as evidence that neurons are not the right unit for most behaviour. They never measure interpretability of non-universal neurons.

statements.correction: Paper: 1-5% of neurons universal across seeds (excess correlation >0.5); 4.16% GPT2-small-a, 1.23% GPT2-medium, 1.26% Pythia-160M (1253/98304 in GPT2-medium-a is 1.27%); selected universal neurons usually have clear interpretations (qualitative).
statements.problem: None. 1-5% overall, 4.16% GPT2-small-a, 1.23% GPT2-medium(-a) and 1.26% Pythia-160M are all in the text. The clear-interpretation claim matches the abstract: it is qualitative and covers only neurons selected by ϱ>0.5.
